name: Raju
definition: Raju is a composite portrait of a skilled foundry mould-maker in Vijayapura city, navigating the pressures of industrial work, rising household costs, and the aspiration to see his children finish schooling in a district where dropout rates and economic volatility test even stable working families. He belongs to the Ganiga sub-caste of Lingayats, a community historically associated with oil-pressing and now spread across trades, farming and wage labour in Vijayapura.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Raju works at a small foundry near the APMC Road that casts agricultural pump parts and motor housings. His day begins at seven-thirty; he prepares sand moulds, pours molten metal under a tin-roofed shed where the heat in summer months is brutal, and finishes moulds by hand with files and scrapers. The foundry employs eight men; wages are paid weekly, about Rs 14,000 a month for Raju, sometimes delayed when orders slow. Metal prices and farmer demand swing with the monsoon: a drought year like 2023 or the feared declaration in 2026 means fewer pump orders and shorter weeks. Diesel, groceries and school fees have all climbed; his wife's ration card helps with rice under Anna Bhagya, but vegetables, kerosene and clinic visits eat into savings. Raju keeps a modest emergency fund in a post-office account and borrowed Rs 40,000 two years ago from a local finance company to repair the house roof; monthly instalments of Rs 2,200 continue. He rides a fifteen-year-old TVS motorcycle to work, shares tea at a stall outside the foundry gate, and returns home by seven in the evening, hands blackened and shoulders aching.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Raju lives in a two-room house with a small courtyard in a Ganiga-majority lane near the railway crossing. His wife Renuka manages the household, cooks on an LPG stove, draws water from a street tap that runs for two hours each morning, and washes clothes by hand. They have three children: a daughter aged eighteen who passed SSLC last year and now stays home helping with housework and younger siblings; a son aged fifteen in Class 10 at a Kannada-medium government high school; and a younger daughter aged eleven in Class 6. Raju's mother, now seventy-two and widowed, lives with them; she suffers joint pain and relies on him for medicines and clinic visits. His elder brother farms a small dryland plot in a village twelve kilometres away; they meet on festival days and sometimes share costs for family ceremonies. Gender roles are traditional: Renuka does not work outside the home, though she once stitched blouses for neighbours; Raju decides major expenses, but Renuka manages the ration card, Gruha Lakshmi instalments and children's clothing. The eldest daughter's marriage is on his mind; arranging it will require a loan or pledging gold.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Raju completed Class 7 in his native village; his parents needed him to work, and schooling ended. He is determined his children will do better. His son Suresh studies at the government boys' high school a kilometre away; fees are low, but notebooks, uniform and a second-hand bicycle cost about Rs 3,000 a year, and Suresh attends evening tuition for mathematics and science at Rs 500 a month. Suresh wants to study PU and join a polytechnic or ITI; Raju hopes he will, though PU college fees, hostel costs and two years without earnings worry him. His younger daughter Kavita studies at a Kannada-medium primary school; she is bright and regular. The eldest, Lata, passed SSLC with 60 per cent but did not continue; Raju could not afford college fees and believed marriage was the next step, a decision he now half-regrets.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Raju's main health concern is his mother's arthritis and his own occasional chest pain from foundry smoke and metal dust. The family uses a government primary health centre for fevers and minor ailments; serious cases mean a trip to the district hospital or a private clinic where consultation and medicines cost Rs 800 to Rs 1,500. His mother's pills for blood pressure cost Rs 300 a month. Raju enrolled in Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka two years ago after a neighbour's hospitalisation; he has not used it yet but keeps the card. Renuka is anaemic, a common issue among women in Vijayapura district according to clinic posters, but she has not had blood tests or regular treatment. Drinking water from the tap sometimes smells of chlorine; during summer, diarrhoea cases rise in the lane, especially among children. Vijayapura's NFHS-5 data show high levels of child stunting and anaemia, though Raju does not follow statistics. Heat is exhausting; last summer he fainted once at the foundry and was given oral rehydration salts. The family has no health insurance beyond Ayushman, and a major illness or accident would mean debt. His mother occasionally visits a traditional bonesetter and uses herbal oil for joint pain, distrusting hospital queues and costs.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Raju belongs to the Ganiga sub-caste within the Lingayat fold, historically oil-pressers, now a small OBC community in Vijayapura. His family visits the Murusavira Math and the Tontadarya Math on festival days and receives prasada. He wears the linga; his wife and mother observe Somavara vrata on Mondays. The lane where he lives is mixed—Ganiga, Kuruba, a few Muslim families—but socialising mostly happens within caste lines. Community ties matter for loans, job leads and marriage arrangements; a Ganiga sangha in the city organises an annual fair and sometimes provides school scholarships, though Raju's children have not received one. He respects the mutt's authority and attended a Panchamasali rally in Belagavi in 2024, though as Ganiga he is not part of that agitation. His Muslim neighbour's son is a friend of Suresh; they play cricket in the street, but Raju would not consider an inter-religious marriage. Renuka participates in a women's self-help group linked to a local NGO; it offers small savings and loans at lower interest than private moneylenders. Raju's trust is in mutts, cooperative banks and kin networks more than government offices, which he finds slow and indifferent.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has a ration card under the National Food Security Act, receiving rice and some sugar; the Gruha Lakshmi Rs 2,000 monthly payment to Renuka has been irregular—delayed twice this year, causing frustration. Shakti free bus travel helped his eldest daughter visit relatives in a nearby village, though city buses are few. Raju has never applied for MGNREGA; it is for villagers, he believes. He once visited the taluk office to get an income certificate for his son's school fee concession; it took three visits and a small payment to a typist. He knows the corporator by face and has asked him twice to fix the street tap; the second time it was done. Raju hears about the Kittur Karnataka development board demand, the winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha, and complaints that Kalyana Karnataka gets Article 371(J) funds while Kittur Karnataka is ignored; he agrees broadly but does not join rallies. His encounters with police are few and wary; once his motorcycle documents were checked and he paid a small fine. Govt schemes feel distant—forms, delays, and favouritism—but the ration card and Ayushman card are tangible.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Raju worries most about money: keeping his son in school, marrying his daughter without crushing debt, and his mother's health. He is proud to be Lingayat, proud of Vijayapura's history—Adil Shahi monuments, Basavanna's vachana legacy—and proud that his children speak Kannada. He resents that Bengaluru and Mysuru get attention, Kalyana Karnataka gets funds, and Kittur Karnataka is left with speeches and a ten-day winter session. Drought, he says, is the city's curse; when rains fail, pump orders vanish, water is rationed, and tempers fray. He blames government negligence for Mahadayi's delay—"Why should Goa get our river?"—and believes Kalasa-Banduri would transform Vijayapura's dry lands, though he is vague on the details. He respects mutts, distrusts politicians equally across parties, and believes hard work and education are the only escape. Outsiders, he says, confuse Vijayapura with the Kalyana or lump it with Belagavi's Marathi politics, missing that it is a Kannada city with its own struggles. He demands Mahadayi water, a Kittur board with real funds, and fair crop prices; he expects little and plans accordingly.
